output:
*Interview with Dr Casimir Vauthier, physician, in the dining room. First day of the year 1900.*

DR VAUTHIER: Forgive me, Inspector. I have a cigar in my fingers and no matches, which is the least of what I am failing at tonight. I have known that house as its doctor and friend for a long time. I sat with Jules Monnier through his last illness in 1889, and I thought then I had seen the worst a family could do to its doctor. I was not prepared for the atelier.

MATTHEY: Take your time, Doctor. I am sorry for your loss.

DR VAUTHIER: Thank you. Aurèle was my oldest friend in this town. Ask me what you need.

MATTHEY: Let us go back to dinner. Do you remember the watches?

DR VAUTHIER: Of course. When the Grand Temple bell struck nine, Aurèle made us all take out our watches, as he does every year, and he told each of us what was wrong with ours. Mine was two minutes ahead of the bell. He said it was the watch of a man who is always early for other people's appointments, and that I would never be a good judge of time. He enjoyed that. So did I.

MATTHEY: And afterwards?

DR VAUTHIER: Odile and I played piquet in the salon. She plays a hard game, Inspector. She takes no prisoners and reads a man's discards the way other women read the newspaper. We played until a quarter to eleven by my watch, when I went out to the hall to fetch my cigar case from my coat.

MATTHEY: Did anything happen as you went out?

DR VAUTHIER: Odile began to play the piano as I went out. It was a nocturne, Chopin, the one she plays when she does not wish to be asked anything. I took my case and went back in, and she stopped when I came back.

MATTHEY: And when did the clock strike?

DR VAUTHIER: The hall clock struck eleven a moment after I sat down again. The old Morbier. It strikes its own hours from its own face and does not wait for anyone's permission. I remember thinking it an odd hour to be keeping us at cards.

MATTHEY: Tell me what you saw of Monnier that night.

DR VAUTHIER: When I saw him, he was already dead, and there was nothing a doctor can do. He had been struck from behind, at the back of the head, with a heavy blow. Death would have been very quick. I will say that plainly, because it is the only comfort I have to offer you, and because I believe it.

MATTHEY: Is there anything more you can tell me about the blow?

DR VAUTHIER: Only that it was given from behind, and given with force. Anything beyond that would be a surgeon's guess, and you are not paying me for guesses.

MATTHEY: Can you tell me the hour of his death?

DR VAUTHIER: No, and I will not pretend I can. I am a physician, not a clock. I can tell you the regulator on the wall had stopped. Stopped with its master, I thought. That is a sentimental thing for a doctor to think, but there it was.

MATTHEY: His repeater was in his hand.

DR VAUTHIER: Yes. He had given that watch his whole attention. He meant it to strike the new century for him, the way a man wants to have the last word. I do not think he would have wished to be found without it. That is what I think about, Inspector, not the blow. Odile would say *de mortuis nil nisi bonum*, and she would be right, though Aurèle was never the easiest man to speak well of.

MATTHEY: Thank you, Doctor. That will be all for now.

DR VAUTHIER: May I have one of your matches first? And tell Odile, if you will, that I lost at piquet and she need not be kind about it.
